node.label: Susan Reynolds
node.date_label: Kingdoms and Communities (1984; second edition 1997) · Fiefs and Vassals (1994) · Before Eminent Domain (2010)
node.description: In Fiefs and Vassals (1994), Susan Reynolds argued that historians had projected later lawyers’ categories of fiefs and vassalage onto earlier medieval relationships, making feudalism a misleading framework. Kingdoms and Communities in Western Europe, 900–1300 (1984; second edition 1997) instead foregrounded collective activity and the political ideas of lay communities, alongside hierarchy and government. Her comparisons challenged the separation of English and continental histories and insisted on distinguishing historians’ terminology from the practices it purported to describe. Reception combined admiration with disagreement: Steven G. Lane’s 1995 review welcomed the reinterpretation but questioned the sharp separation between customary and professional law and the denial of precise meanings to earlier legal vocabulary. In 2012 Reynolds acknowledged corrections by Fredric L. Cheyette and Susan Wood while maintaining her criticism of the non-Marxist feudal framework. Her contribution included studying consultation and collective judgement without equating them with equality or democracy.
node.representative_figures_and_works: An Introduction to the History of English Medieval Towns (1977); “Medieval urban history and the history of political thought” (1982); Kingdoms and Communities in Western Europe, 900–1300 (1984; second edition 1997); “Social mentalities and the case of medieval scepticism” (1991); Fiefs and Vassals (1994); Ideas and Solidarities of the Medieval Laity (1995); “The idea of the nation as a political community” (2005); Before Eminent Domain (2010); The Middle Ages without Feudalism (2012).
node.scope_note: The 1984 and 1994 monographs and Before Eminent Domain were not read in full. Read selected institutional memoir passages, the displayed 1995 review, authorized 1995 and 2012 prefaces, and selected 1991 article passages through p. 36. The 1982 article and 2005 chapter were read only as publisher extracts or summaries. Duby’s books and Smith’s 1973 text remain unread. The IHR interview and Wikidata item could not be accessed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Fiefs and Vassals (1994), Reynolds challenged the feudal framework associated with Bloch’s Feudal Society (1939–1940), according to d’Avray and Hudson’s 2022 memoir.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Named-reader route: d’Avray and Hudson, printed p. 153, paragraph beginning “During this time,” explicitly identifies Bloch’s Feudal Society among her targets. Read the memoir passage and the 1994 publisher abstract; neither complete book was read. This is a bounded critique of the feudal interpretation, not a rejection of Bloch’s entire method.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Social mentalities and the case of medieval scepticism” (1991), Reynolds questions Duby’s inference from religious art to a society’s shared faith in Le Temps des Cathédrales (1976).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary passage read in the authorized 1995 reprint, essay I, p. 26, especially the question containing “pathetic fallacy,” with notes 19–20. She also faults Duby’s limited treatment of unbelief. At p. 31, note 37, she accepts his warning against imposing modern mental attitudes: this is selective criticism. Duby’s complete 1976 book and 1981 translation unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Challenges an inference of universal belief

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The idea of the nation as a political community” (2005), Reynolds explicitly derives her working definition of the nation from Anthony D. Smith’s 1973 formulation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core displayed Summary, third sentence: the definition “lit up the subject for me in a flash.” The displayed passage identifies a specific debt, not membership in an entire theoretical school. The rest of Reynolds’s chapter and Smith’s 1973 text were not read; no title is assigned to that unread Smith text.
proposed_edges.map_label: Credits Smith’s definition of the nation

proposed_edges.relationship: Janet Nelson’s funeral address, quoted in d’Avray and Hudson’s 2022 memoir of Reynolds, credits their discussions with helping Nelson refine and develop historical ideas.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Memoir p. 164, quoted funeral address, final sentence: “helping me refine and develop many ideas.” The surrounding paragraph identifies repeated intellectual discussions at the IHR Early Medieval Seminar. This goes beyond attendance or friendship, but names no particular Nelson publication; no book-specific influence is inferred. Address delivered after Reynolds’s 2021 death, published here in 2022. Nelson is another candidate in this run.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Medieval urban history and the history of political thought” (1982), Reynolds calls for urban historians to study political thought alongside the institutional and material history of towns.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core opening extract, p. 14: paragraph beginning “One of the problems of urban history,” through the proposal to add the history of political thought. Footnote 1 links the argument to collective action and dates its delivery to 1981. Only the displayed extract, metadata and notes were read; no claim about the complete article’s demonstration.
proposed_edges.map_label: Brings political thought into urban history

proposed_edges.relationship: In the preface to The Middle Ages without Feudalism (2012), Reynolds renews Kingdoms and Communities (1984)’s emphasis on collective values, consultation and judgement in medieval government.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary 2012 preface xiv, paragraphs beginning “However many mistakes,” “To those,” and “I nevertheless think.” She expressly says collective government was not egalitarian or democratic and could protect higher-status interests. The 1984 book was not read in full; this is her later explicit restatement.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the preface to Ideas and Solidarities of the Medieval Laity (1995), Reynolds describes reconstructing lay political ideas from collective activities, a project developed in Kingdoms and Communities (1984).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary 1995 preface vii–viii: opening paragraph explains the move from English towns to their inhabitants’ ideas about society and politics, then to people outside towns; the next paragraph stresses lay capacities for “rational and independent thought.” Read this preface, not the whole collection or 1984 book. Contribution to the field is an editorial mapping of that explicit programme, not a claim of Cambridge School affiliation.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The idea of the nation as a political community” (2005), Reynolds argues that a conception of nations as natural political communities was widespread before the eighteenth century.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core displayed Summary, opening and closing sentences. Her claim concerns a conception of political community; she explicitly withholds the inference that earlier people shared modern nationalists’ aims and policies. Only the summary and publication metadata were read. Mapping to nationalism studies follows the named subject and argument, not shared chronology alone.

proposed_edges.relationship: According to Sarah B. Lynch, Barbara H. Rosenwein’s Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006) extended Susan Reynolds’s account of overlapping communities in Kingdoms and Communities in Western Europe, 900–1300 (1984; second edition 1997).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Lynch’s discussion of interlocking communities and note 93. This is an explicit secondary attribution of extension, attached to substantive body analysis. The cited Rosenwein page and Reynolds book were not directly read; no claim that Reynolds originated emotional communities.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Society: hierarchy and solidarity” (2015), Susan Reynolds contributed to world history by comparing inequality and the relationship between social hierarchy and solidarity across societies of the Middle Millennium.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher summary and volume contents. Claim limited to the stated comparative argument; full chapter unread. The British Academy memoir independently discusses this chapter’s extension across world history (p. 158). This records a specific field contribution, without asserting subsequent uptake.
proposed_edges.map_label: Compares hierarchy and solidarity across societies
